power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Flaws in Navarro, Pathare, and Rossi's (2026) "Theory-Driven" Reanalysis of Paap et al. (2026): An Analytic Reconstruction

text.text: This commentary concerns Navarro, Pathare, and Rossi's (2026) reanalysis of data originally reported by Paap et al. (2026).
text.formatted: This commentary concerns Navarro, Pathare, and <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Rossi's (2026)</ref> reanalysis of data originally reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Paap et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: An earlier version was submitted to Psychological Review as a Theoretical Note.
The present version is posted as a preprint to make the analytic reconstruction and associated concerns available for scholarly evaluation.
The authors have also brought the issues concerning the published record to the attention of the Editor of Psychological Review and APA.

Reproducibility materials are provided as supplementary material and include the source data, audit script, principal analytic outputs, independent multiple-imputation pooling validation, and session information from the completed reconstruction.

Keywords: theory testing, bilingualism, executive functioning, multiple imputation, falsifiability Calling an analysis theory-driven conveys more than the claim that theory influenced decisions about what variables to measure or how to organize them.

In its stronger and more scientifically consequential sense, theory-driven research uses theory to constrain what should be observed: the theory identifies relationships expected before the data are examined, distinguishes those outcomes from plausible alternatives, and thereby creates some empirical result that would count against the theoretical account.
Without such constraints, theory can guide decisions about the selection, transformation, and interpretation of variables while remaining sufficiently flexible to accommodate many possible outcomes.

We refer to this role of theory as theory-guided analysis: theory helps construct or interpret an analysis, but the analysis need not provide the advance constraints required for a severe test of the theory.
Theory testing, by contrast, requires predictions sufficiently constrained that plausible outcomes can be identified in advance that would count against the theoretical account.
Both forms of inquiry may contribute to scientific progress, but they make different epistemic claims.

This distinction parallels two influential perspectives on scientific progress that are particularly relevant to the present case. Oberauer and Lewandowsky (2019), in addressing psychology's 'theory crisis,' distinguished discovery-oriented research from theory testing, arguing that theory testing requires theories that strongly imply hypotheses such that disconfirmation of those hypotheses provides evidence against the theory. Navarro-Torres et al. (2021), in turn, advocated a discovery-science approach to bilingualism, emphasizing the value of characterizing the multidimensional variability of bilingual experience and using observed patterns to generate and refine theoretical accounts.
text.formatted: This distinction parallels two influential perspectives on scientific progress that are particularly relevant to the present case. <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Oberauer and Lewandowsky (2019)</ref>, in addressing psychology's 'theory crisis,' distinguished discovery-oriented research from theory testing, arguing that theory testing requires theories that strongly imply hypotheses such that disconfirmation of those hypotheses provides evidence against the theory. <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Navarro-Torres et al. (2021)</ref>, in turn, advocated a discovery-science approach to bilingualism, emphasizing the value of characterizing the multidimensional variability of bilingual experience and using observed patterns to generate and refine theoretical accounts.

text.text: We view these approaches as complementary rather than competing.
Complementarity, however, implies progression as well as coexistence: discoveries should eventually support theories sufficiently constrained to face informative tests.

Discovery science can identify phenomena and candidate relationships that theory must eventually explain; theory testing asks whether a theoretical account predicted and constrained those relationships before they were observed.

The difficulty arises when an analysis that retains the exploratory flexibility of discovery science is presented as a stronger test of theory merely because theoretical considerations guided its construction and interpretation.

A recently published reanalysis by Navarro et al. (2026) provides an unusually useful case in which to examine this distinction. Navarro et al. reanalyzed data originally reported by Paap et al. (2026), arguing that a more theory-driven treatment of individual differences in bilingual experience reveals relationships with executive functioning (EF) that were obscured by the original approach.
text.formatted: A recently published reanalysis by <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Navarro et al. (2026)</ref> provides an unusually useful case in which to examine this distinction. <ref type="bibr">Navarro et al.</ref> reanalyzed data originally reported by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Paap et al. (2026)</ref>, arguing that a more theory-driven treatment of individual differences in bilingual experience reveals relationships with executive functioning (EF) that were obscured by the original approach.

text.text: Their critique is consequential because it challenges not simply particular analytic choices but the logic of the original test: the sample was characterized as lacking appropriate theoretical grounding, the measures of bilingual experience as insufficiently theory motivated, and the analytic approach as suboptimal.

Their reanalysis restricted the sample, reconstructed several measures of bilingual experience, reorganized those measures into three latent factors, and reported in the text of their results and discussion that two of those factors significantly predicted EF.
This exchange raises two separable questions.
First, does Navarro et al.'s reanalysis provide a more severe test of theoretically specified predictions than the original analysis?
Second, do the empirical results reported by Navarro et al. support the conclusions drawn from them?
We conclude that the answer to both questions is no.
Some of the changes described as theoretically motivated were not uniquely dictated by theory and, in several instances, introduce new measurement problems.

More importantly, our reconstruction of Navarro et al.'s analyses from their publicly available code reveals discrepancies between the published description of their results and the results produced by that code.
The supplied code generates 20 multiply imputed datasets but then fits the reported structural model to only imputation #5 rather than pooling estimates and uncertainty across the 20 imputations.

Our reconstruction using imputation #5 reproduces the standardized coefficients and factor loadings in Navarro et al.'s Figure 5 with striking precision, providing a strong check that we have identified the analysis underlying the published figure.
text.formatted: Our reconstruction using imputation #5 reproduces the standardized coefficients and factor loadings in Navarro et al.'s Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> with striking precision, providing a strong check that we have identified the analysis underlying the published figure.

text.text: In that reconstruction, only the Timing/Duration-to-EF path is statistically significant.
However, the path is no longer significant when we fit the same model to all 20 imputations and combine the estimates and uncertainty using Rubin's (1987) rules.
text.formatted: However, the path is no longer significant when we fit the same model to all 20 imputations and combine the estimates and uncertainty using <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Rubin's (1987)</ref> rules.

text.text: An independent FIML analysis we conducted yields the same conclusion: none of the three bilingualism factors significantly predicts EF.
These empirical problems matter in their own right, and because the reanalysis appeared in the same journal as the original article, we believe that clarifying the published record is important.
But the broader significance of the case is methodological and theoretical.

A reanalysis can be informed by an elaborate theoretical framework, employ sophisticated latentvariable models, and produce interpretable relations among constructs without necessarily providing a severe test of that framework.
The critical question is not simply whether theory motivated the analysis, but how much the theory constrained the result before it was known.
The Navarro et al. reanalysis therefore provides an opportunity to examine a more general problem in psychological science: when does theoretical guidance become theory testing?

The Theoretical Test in Paap et al. (2026) The characterization of Paap et al. (2026) as insufficiently theory driven is surprising because the central analysis was designed to test a longstanding theoretical claim about bilingual experience and domain-general cognitive control.
text.formatted: The Theoretical Test in <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Paap et al. (2026)</ref> The characterization of <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Paap et al. (2026)</ref> as insufficiently theory driven is surprising because the central analysis was designed to test a longstanding theoretical claim about bilingual experience and domain-general cognitive control.

text.text: Although formulations of the bilingual advantage hypothesis have varied, Bialystok (2024) recently provided an unusually concise statement of the proposed mechanism.
text.formatted: Although formulations of the bilingual advantage hypothesis have varied, <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">Bialystok (2024)</ref> recently provided an unusually concise statement of the proposed mechanism.

text.text: She argues that "the jointly activated languages in bilingual minds place constant demands on selective attention, an underlying resource."
With experience, "attention is subsequently modified, becoming more efficient in that the limited resource can be used more effectively."

Critically, the proposed consequence extends beyond language: "this modification is seen indirectly in more efficient performance on a range of tasks that require high levels of selective attention" (p. 1).

Thus, the proposed causal sequence is explicit: repeated bilingual language-control demands → increased efficiency of a domaingeneral attentional resource → superior performance on tasks that tax that resource.

These statements are particularly useful for theory testing because they specify not merely an association between bilingualism and EF, but the experience, the proposed mechanism of change, and the behavioral consequence of that change.

The EF side of the model was designed in response to a major weakness of much of the preceding bilingual-advantage literature: the poor reliability and convergent validity of traditional interference scores.

Three of the five indicators were the Flanker Squared, Simon Squared, and Stroop Squared tasks developed specifically to improve the psychometric measurement of attentional control (Burgoyne et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Three of the five indicators were the Flanker Squared, Simon Squared, and Stroop Squared tasks developed specifically to improve the psychometric measurement of attentional control <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Burgoyne et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In the original validation work these measures showed substantially improved test-retest reliability and convergent validity, and their strong intercorrelations replicated in the Paap et al. sample.

Thus, failure to observe the predicted relationship could not readily be attributed to the familiar objection that EF had been measured with unreliable difference scores that failed to converge on a common construct.
Bilingualism was likewise treated not as a binary demographic category but as a continuous, multidimensional experience.

The latent construct incorporated proficiency, relative proficiency, switching frequency, diversity of language use across seven everyday contexts, balance of language use, and number of languages spoken.
These indicators loaded strongly on a common bilingualism factor, yet that factor did not predict the latent EF factor: the standardized path was approximately -.05.
Importantly, the evidence against the predicted advantage did not rest solely on nonsignificant frequentist tests.

In complementary bilingual-monolingual comparisons, Bayes factors favored the null for all five performance-based EF measures, with the three psychometrically strongest Squared measures providing substantial evidence for the null.

Additional Bayesian analyses examining the relationships of L2 age of acquisition and years of L2 experience with each of the 10 EF and self-control measures likewise favored the null in all 20 comparisons (all BF₀₁ > 3; mean BF₀₁ = 8.0).
text.formatted: Additional Bayesian analyses examining the relationships of L2 age of acquisition and years of L2 experience with each of the 10 EF and self-control measures likewise favored the null in all 20 comparisons (all BF₀₁ > 3; mean BF₀₁ = 8.0).

text.text: Consequently, the null relationship was not discovered in the absence of a theoretical prediction, nor was it inferred merely from a failure to reject the null hypothesis.

It was the outcome of a test constructed to give a prominent theoretical prediction a comparatively favorable opportunity to succeed, with complementary Bayesian analyses providing evidence favoring the null over the predicted bilingual advantage.
There are two distinct problems with this assertion.
First, the descriptive characteristics of Paap et al.'s bilingual participants (see their Table 2) are difficult to reconcile with the characterization "largely imbalanced."
text.formatted: First, the descriptive characteristics of Paap et al.'s bilingual participants (see their Table <ref type="table">2</ref>) are difficult to reconcile with the characterization "largely imbalanced."

text.text: Their mean proficiency in the second-most proficient language is 5.7 on a scale where 6.0 is labeled "as proficient as a native speaker," their mean P2/P1 is .89, the mean number of languages used across the seven contexts was 1.7, and the mean number of language switches is more than a dozen times per day.
On average they report using their P2 about one-third of the time.
It is hard to construe this profile as "largely unbalanced."
Second, restricting that same sample, as Navarro et al. did, to a subset of participants does not create additional experience that was absent from the original dataset.
It changes which portion of the existing distribution is analyzed.

Such a restriction may be defensible for a particular theoretical question, but its theoretical status should be explicit: what feature of the theory predicts that the relationship should emerge within the selected bilingual range but not across the broader continuum?
Without such a prediction, restricting the sample is a theorycompatible analytic choice rather than a consequence uniquely dictated by the theory.
The more consequential changes involve the bilingualism indicators themselves.
Navarro et al. retained some information from the original measures but reconstructed other indicators before entering them into their factor analysis.
Three changes are particularly important because each illustrates the distinction between invoking theory to justify a measure and demonstrating that the theory requires that operationalization.
First, Navarro et al. calculated language entropy from participants' overall percentages of language use.

Shannon entropy is a legitimate measure of the diversity or balance of a probability distribution, but this operationalization differs importantly from the contextual entropy measure used by Paap et al. (2026).
text.formatted: Shannon entropy is a legitimate measure of the diversity or balance of a probability distribution, but this operationalization differs importantly from the contextual entropy measure used by <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Paap et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: The original measure quantified uncertainty in language use across seven everyday contexts and was intended to capture the degree to which language selection varies with context.
Collapsing across contexts produces a measure primarily sensitive to the overall distribution of language use.

A bilingual who uses one language almost exclusively at home and another almost exclusively at school or work can therefore resemble a bilingual who mixes the two languages broadly across contexts, despite potentially quite different language-control experiences.
If contextual demands are central to the proposed mechanism of adaptation, eliminating context is not transparently a theoretical improvement.
Second, Navarro et al.'s timing/duration factor is defined by L2 age of acquisition (AoA) and years of simultaneous language use.
The latter is calculated in part from the former.
Consequently, covariance between the two indicators arises partly by mathematical construction rather than necessarily because both independently reflect a common latent psychological dimension.

This does not by itself invalidate the factor, but it complicates its interpretation as evidence for a coherent underlying timing/duration construct-particularly when only two indicators define that construct.
Third, the proficiency variables require careful attention to the meaning of the original measures.
P1 and P2 in the Paap et al. dataset designated participants' most proficient and second-most-proficient languages, respectively; they did not necessarily designate L1 and L2.
Treating those measures as though they straightforwardly index proficiency in chronologically defined first and second languages changes the meaning of the variables.
A theoretically motivated model cannot improve measurement simply by assigning a theoretically desirable interpretation to an indicator that differs from what was actually measured.

Navarro et al. subsequently used exploratory factor analysis to organize the reconstructed bilingualism indicators into three dimensions that they interpreted as language use/intensity, proficiency, and timing/duration.
There is nothing inherently objectionable about exploratory factor analysis; indeed, it can be useful when the dimensional structure of a construct is uncertain.
But its role matters for the claim that the resulting analysis is theory driven.

To the extent that the number and composition of the factors were determined by patterns observed in these data, the latent structure was at least partly discovered from the dataset rather than specified by the theory before the dataset was examined.
That is entirely appropriate for discovery science, but it matters for the stronger claim that the resulting analysis constitutes a theory test.
This is precisely where the distinction introduced at the outset becomes consequential.
UBET and related frameworks may make the resulting factors theoretically interpretable after they have been identified.

That establishes theoretical coherence, but it is not equivalent to demonstrating that the theory predicted this particular factor structure rather than other plausible organizations of the same indicators.
A latent-variable solution can therefore be both empirically sensible and theoretically interpretable while remaining theory guided rather than constituting a severe test of that theory.
A related problem concerns Navarro et al.'s formal comparisons between their reconstructed models and the models they describe as replications of Paap et al. (2026).
text.formatted: A related problem concerns Navarro et al.'s formal comparisons between their reconstructed models and the models they describe as replications of <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Paap et al. (2026)</ref>.

text.text: The supplied code uses likelihood-ratio tests to compare the new three-factor CFA with the replicated CFA and, later, the new SEM with the replicated SEM.
These comparisons do not involve nested models fitted to the same observed variables and the same observations: the models differ in their indicators and analytic samples.
Consequently, the resulting chi-square difference tests do not provide valid tests that one model fits better than the other.
For the same reason, differences in AIC and BIC across models fitted to different data cannot be interpreted as evidence that the reconstructed model provides superior fit.

This does not bear on whether Navarro et al.'s reconstructed models are reasonable representations of their selected data; it bears on the stronger claim that the reported model comparisons demonstrate an empirical improvement over the models they were intended to replace.
Multiple imputation is well suited to this type of missing-data problem because it does not treat any single set of imputed values as though those values were actually observed.
Instead, multiple completed datasets are generated to represent plausible values for the missing observations.
The statistical model is then fitted separately to each completed dataset, and the resulting parameter estimates and their uncertainty are combined using Rubin's rules.
The between-imputation variability is essential: it represents uncertainty about values that were not observed (Rubin, 1987; van Buuren, 2018).
text.formatted: The between-imputation variability is essential: it represents uncertainty about values that were not observed <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Rubin, 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">van Buuren, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The original Paap et al. (2026) data and analysis materials are publicly archived on OSF (https://osf.io/j8gvh/?view_only=9ffe42c84278487d9f541efd3ef1a44c).
text.formatted: The original <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Paap et al. (2026)</ref> data and analysis materials are publicly archived on OSF (<ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/j8gvh/?view_only=9ffe42c84278487d9f541efd3ef1a44c">https://osf.io/j8gvh/?view_only=9ffe42c84278487d9f541efd3ef1a44c</ref>).

text.text: This distinction is consequential in the present case.
Inspection of the code supplied by Navarro et al. shows that 20 imputed datasets are generated, but the subsequent structural equation model is not fitted to all 20 and the estimates are not pooled.
text.formatted: Inspection of the code supplied by <ref type="bibr">Navarro et al.</ref> shows that 20 imputed datasets are generated, but the subsequent structural equation model is not fitted to all 20 and the estimates are not pooled.

text.text: Instead, the code uses the complete() function to extract completed dataset #5, and the reported SEM is then fitted to that single completed dataset.
Thus, although multiple imputation was performed, the inferential advantage of multiple imputation was not carried forward into the structural analysis.
Once a single completed dataset is treated as the dataset for purposes of estimation and inference, uncertainty attributable to the missing values is omitted.
Identifying dataset #5 in the supplied code would not by itself establish that it was the dataset underlying the results reported by Navarro et al.
We therefore attempted to reconstruct their published model directly.

Using the supplied data and code, we fitted their specified SEM to completed dataset #5 and compared the resulting estimates with those displayed in Figure 5 of That reconstruction also permits the statistical significance of the paths to be examined directly.
text.formatted: Using the supplied data and code, we fitted their specified SEM to completed dataset #5 and compared the resulting estimates with those displayed in Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> of That reconstruction also permits the statistical significance of the paths to be examined directly.

text.text: The β values reported here are standardized effect sizes; the accompanying p values test the corresponding unstandardized SEM path coefficients.
In our reconstruction, the Factor 1 → EF path is β = -.204, p = .308; the Factor 2 → EF path is β = .050, p = .793; and the Factor 3 → EF path is β = .207, p = .037.
Thus, only the Factor 3 path is statistically significant in our reconstruction of the analysis underlying Figure 5.
text.formatted: Thus, only the Factor 3 path is statistically significant in our reconstruction of the analysis underlying Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>.

text.text: Table 1 places this reconstruction alongside Navarro et al.'s published descriptions of the same paths and the two additional missing-data analyses reported below.

The resulting pattern reveals two distinct discrepancies: inconsistencies within the published report itself, and a change in the inferential conclusion once uncertainty due to missing data is appropriately incorporated.
This result exposes an additional discrepancy in the published report.
Navarro et al. state in the Results that both Factor 1 and Factor 3 have significant regression paths to EF and describe the Factor 1 path as positive (.20) and the Factor 3 path as negative (-.21).
Figure 5 shows the opposite signs: Factor 1 → EF is approximately -.20 and Factor 3 → EF approximately +.21.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> shows the opposite signs: Factor 1 → EF is approximately -.20 and Factor 3 → EF approximately +.21.

text.text: Our reconstruction reproduces the signs shown in their Figure 5 rather than those stated in their Results.
text.formatted: Our reconstruction reproduces the signs shown in their Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> rather than those stated in their Results.

text.text: More importantly, our reconstruction provides no support for the statement that the Factor 1 path is statistically significant.
Its p value is .308.
The Factor 3 path, by contrast, is significant in completed dataset #5 (p = .037), consistent with the significance claim but not with the sign given in the Results.
The distinction is important.
The problem is not merely that signs appear to have been transposed in the prose.
The published article characterizes two bilingualism factors as significantly related to EF, whereas our reconstruction of the analysis underlying its Figure 5 identifies only one significant path.
text.formatted: The published article characterizes two bilingualism factors as significantly related to EF, whereas our reconstruction of the analysis underlying its Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref> identifies only one significant path.

text.text: The remaining question is whether the significant Factor 3 effect is robust to the uncertainty that multiple imputation was intended to represent.
To answer that question, we fitted the same SEM separately to each of the 20 completed datasets generated by the Navarro et al.
imputation procedure.
We then pooled the three unstandardized structural coefficients and their standard errors using Rubin's rules.
The pooled results were clear.
For Factor 1 → EF, the pooled estimate was b = -.012, p = .951.
For Factor 2 → EF, it was b = -.054, p = .690.
For Factor 3 → EF-the only significant path in the reconstruction using completed dataset #5-the pooled estimate was b = .099, p = .256.
Thus, none of the three bilingualism factors significantly predicts EF when the estimates and uncertainty are appropriately combined across the 20 imputed datasets.
The change in the Factor 3 inference illustrates why pooling is not an optional technical refinement.
Dataset #5 happens to yield an estimate sufficiently large relative to its withindataset standard error to cross the conventional significance threshold.
But it is only one plausible completed version of a dataset containing substantial missing EF information.
The 19 other imputations contain different plausible replacements for those missing observations.
Rubin's rules incorporate both the uncertainty within each completed dataset and the variability of the estimates across completed datasets.
The significant Factor 3 path in imputation #5 therefore does not represent a pathway that survives the multiple-imputation procedure that Navarro et al. themselves initiated.
As a complementary analysis, we fitted the same SEM directly to the original incomplete dataset using full-information maximum likelihood (FIML).
Unlike multiple imputation, FIML does not create completed datasets.

Instead, it estimates the model directly from all of the observed information available for each participant, allowing individuals with partially missing data to contribute whatever information they provide.
FIML, like multiple imputation, does not require data to be missing completely at random.

Under an appropriately specified model, FIML can yield valid estimates under the weaker missing-at-random (MAR) assumption: conditional on the variables included in the model, the probability that an observation is missing must not depend further on the unobserved value itself (Enders, 2010).
text.formatted: Under an appropriately specified model, FIML can yield valid estimates under the weaker missing-at-random (MAR) assumption: conditional on the variables included in the model, the probability that an observation is missing must not depend further on the unobserved value itself <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Enders, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: In the Paap et al. data, much of the missing EF information arose because participants completed the initial online Qualtrics session but did not subsequently come to campus for the separate laboratory session in which the performance-based EF tasks and MINT were administered.
Thus, much of the missingness reflects a procedural transition between phases of the study rather than selective noncompletion of particular EF tasks.

At the same time, return to the laboratory may have depended on characteristics such as availability, motivation, need for additional research participation credit, or other participant attributes that may not be fully represented in the SEM.
We therefore do not assume that MAR is guaranteed.
Rather, FIML serves here as a methodologically distinct sensitivity analysis.
Its results closely converge with the pooled multiple-imputation analysis: Factor 1 → EF, β = .061, p = .779; Factor 2 → EF, β = -.153, p = .449; and Factor 3 → EF, β = .118, p = .281.
Once again, none of the three bilingualism factors significantly predicts EF.
The sequence of results is therefore unusually informative.
Our reconstruction of completed dataset #5 reproduces Navarro et al.'s published Figure 5, establishing that we can recover the analysis underlying the figure.
text.formatted: Our reconstruction of completed dataset #5 reproduces Navarro et al.'s published Figure <ref type="figure">5</ref>, establishing that we can recover the analysis underlying the figure.

text.text: That reconstruction supports a significant relationship between Factor 3 and EF but not the reported significant relationship between Factor 1 and EF.
When we extend the same analysis to all 20 datasets generated by
Navarro et al.'s multipleimputation procedure and properly pool the results, the Factor 3 relationship is no longer significant.
When we instead analyze the incomplete data using FIML, the same conclusion follows.
Across two appropriate approaches to the missing data, none of Navarro et al.'s three reconstructed dimensions of bilingual experience significantly predicts EF.
This does not imply that the true relationships are exactly zero, nor does it establish evidence for a point null merely from nonsignificant p values.

It establishes the narrower-but consequential-conclusion relevant to the published claim: the evidence reported by Navarro et al. does not support the conclusion that their theoretically motivated reanalysis recovered significant relationships between bilingual experience and EF that were obscured in the original Paap et al. analysis.
The empirical reconstruction raises a broader question that is independent of the discrepancies in the reported analyses.
Suppose, for purposes of argument, that the relationships reported by Navarro et al. had survived appropriate treatment of the missing data.
Would the resulting pattern have constituted a stronger test of theory?

Following Oberauer and Lewandowsky (2019), answering that question requires identifying what the theoretical framework predicted before the observed relationships were known and which plausible outcomes would have provided evidence against it.
Navarro et al. invoke UBET and the ACH to motivate a multidimensional representation of bilingual experience.
Both frameworks provide reasons to expect that different features of bilingual experience may be associated with different forms of cognitive or neural adaptation.
That is a useful theoretical perspective.

But a framework that identifies many potentially relevant dimensions of experience does not thereby specify which dimensions should predict a particular behavioral outcome, in what direction, or under what conditions.
The distinction matters in the present case because Navarro et al.'s three bilingualism factors provide several opportunities for theoretically interpretable outcomes.
Greater language use or switching could be associated with better EF because repeated control demands strengthen domain-general control.
But a weak or absent association could be attributed to automatization, insufficient control demands, or the possibility that adaptation is specific to language rather than domain general.

Timing and duration could positively predict EF because earlier or more prolonged bilingual experience provides greater opportunity for adaptation; alternatively, later acquisition could impose greater control demands and therefore produce greater adaptation.

Proficiency could predict EF if successful management of two highly active languages taxes control, but an absent proficiency relationship could also be accommodated if proficiency reduces rather than increases control demands.
The problem is not that any of these explanations is intrinsically implausible.
The problem is that their availability after the result is known makes it difficult to identify which result would have challenged the theoretical account.
A framework becomes a testable theory not merely by providing an explanation for an observed relationship, but by excluding plausible alternatives before the data are examined.
The issue is particularly visible in the relationship between This example is complicated further by the construction of the switching indicator.
Navarro et al. combined switching per day with switching within sentences.
Yet these forms of switching need not instantiate the same control demands.

Under the ACH, dense code-switching is associated with an open-control mode in which elements from either language may be opportunistically selected, reducing demands on the competitive control processes emphasized in single-language and especially dual-language contexts (Green & Abutalebi, 2013).
text.formatted: Under the ACH, dense code-switching is associated with an open-control mode in which elements from either language may be opportunistically selected, reducing demands on the competitive control processes emphasized in single-language and especially dual-language contexts <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Green & Abutalebi, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Although within-utterance switching need not uniformly instantiate dense code-switching, Navarro et al.'s composite therefore combines switching behaviors that cannot be assumed to represent equivalent-or even monotonically increasing-amounts of the control experience proposed to produce adaptation.

If the theoretical mechanism is repeated exercise of control, combining these heterogeneous forms of switching into a single indicator makes its relationship to the proposed mechanism-and therefore its directional prediction for EF-ambiguous.
The same logical issue extends beyond any one indicator.
Once multiple experience dimensions are available, positive, negative, and null relationships can often be given theoretically coherent interpretations.

A positive association may indicate adaptation to repeated demands; a null association may indicate automatization or insufficient generalization; and a negative association may be interpreted as greater efficiency, reduced need for control, or adaptation along some other dimension.
Such explanations may prove correct.

But when the mechanism responsible for each outcome is selected only after the outcome has been observed, the explanatory flexibility of the framework has increased while its capacity for severe testing has decreased.
This is why the distinction between theory-guided analysis and theory testing is consequential rather than semantic.
UBET and ACH clearly guided Navarro et al.'s thinking about which aspects of bilingual experience might matter and how observed relationships might be interpreted.
What is less clear is what pattern among the three bilingualism factors and EF was predicted strongly enough that a materially different pattern would have counted against the account.
If F1 had positively predicted EF, would that have supported the theory?
If F3 rather than F1 predicted EF, would that also have supported it?
If proficiency alone predicted EF?
If the coefficients had the opposite signs?
If none predicted EF?
These are not rhetorical questions.
They identify the information required to distinguish a theoretical prediction from a theoretically compatible outcome.

A theory that can explain several possible results may still be useful, but the evidential value of obtaining any one of those results depends on how strongly the theory favored it over the alternatives before the result was known.
There is a still broader version of the problem.
As theoretical frameworks become richer, they often identify more potentially relevant experiences, mechanisms, moderators, and outcomes.
This richness can improve description and generate productive hypotheses.
But it also creates what might be called a selection problem: which of the many theoretically plausible mechanisms should be selected to generate a prediction for the case at hand?
The selection problem cannot be solved merely by showing after the fact that the observed result is consistent with one component of the framework.

To generate a risky prediction, the theory must provide some basis for selecting that mechanism before the result is observed and for explaining why competing mechanisms should not dominate under those conditions.
Otherwise, the researcher-not the theory-performs the crucial act of selection after seeing the data.
This distinction helps clarify why increasingly elaborate theoretical frameworks can sometimes become more difficult rather than easier to test.
Adding mechanisms increases explanatory resources.
Unless the theory also specifies the conditions under which each mechanism operates, however, those additional resources enlarge the set of outcomes that can be accommodated.
Explanatory breadth and empirical constraint are therefore not the same achievement.
The remedy is not to demand implausibly precise quantitative predictions from every psychological theory.
A useful theory can make ordinal or directional predictions, specify boundary conditions, or identify observations that should be substantially more likely under one account than another.
Nor must every study constitute a decisive falsification attempt.
Exploratory analyses and theory-guided discovery are indispensable parts of science.
As Navarro-Torres et al. (2021) emphasize, discovery science is indispensable for characterizing the heterogeneity of bilingual experience and identifying relationships worthy of explanation.

text.text: The requirement is not that discovery be replaced by confirmatory theory testing, but that the epistemic claim match the analysis.
Our concern is not that Navarro et al. engaged in discovery.
It is that analytic decisions characteristic of discovery science were presented as providing a more stringent test of theory without specifying the outcomes that the theory excluded in advance.
If theory was used to identify potentially meaningful variables and interpret relationships discovered among them, theory-guided is an accurate and valuable description.

If the analysis is presented as a stronger test of theory, the additional question must be answered: What reasonably possible result would have led us to conclude that the theoretical account was wrong, incomplete, or in need of revision?
That question brings the Navarro et al. reanalysis full circle.
Their reanalysis was clearly informed by contemporary theories of bilingual experience.

But the theoretically motivated reconstruction of variables, data-informed extraction of latent dimensions, and post hoc interpretation of their relationships with EF do not by themselves make the analysis a more severe theoretical test than the one it was intended to replace.

Indeed, Paap et al. began with a comparatively simple directional prediction derived from the proposed mechanism: if increasingly bilingual experience modifies a domain-general attentional resource, greater bilingual experience should predict better performance on reliable measures of that resource.
The failure of that prediction is theoretically informative precisely because the opposite result was not equally predicted.
The broader lesson extends beyond bilingualism.
Psychological theories increasingly accommodate heterogeneity by adding mechanisms, moderators, contexts, and developmental trajectories.
Such elaboration can represent theoretical progress, but only when it increases constraint as well as explanatory reach.
A framework that identifies many processes capable of producing different outcomes does not become more testable merely because each observed outcome can subsequently be connected to one of them.
Progress requires specifying, before the result is known, which mechanism should dominate under the conditions at hand and what observations would count against that prediction.
Theories earn evidential support not simply by explaining what happened, but by taking the risk that something else could have happened instead.
Unless that increased richness eventually produces greater constraint, accumulating discoveries can perversely make a theory harder rather than easier to test.
The question, therefore, is not whether bilingualism research still has discoveries to make-it plainly doesbut whether decades of discovery have produced theories capable of being wrong.
That theoretical claim places unusually clear requirements on an informative test.
The measure of bilingual experience should capture variation in the experiences proposed to generate adaptation rather than merely divide participants into nominal bilingual and monolingual groups.
The measures of EF should reliably capture the domain-general ability purportedly modified by that experience.
And, most importantly, greater bilingual experience should positively predict the EF construct.
Paap et al. attempted to satisfy precisely those requirements.

This does not imply that every measurement decision in Paap et al. was uniquely dictated by theory; the critical constraint was the directional prediction linking greater bilingual experience to better domaingeneral EF.

Navarro et al. (2026) frame their reanalysis as an application of the Unified Bilingual Experience Trajectories (UBET) framework(DeLuca et al., 2020), informed as well by the Adaptive Control Hypothesis (ACH;Green & Abutalebi, 2013).

text.text: The general motivation is reasonable.
Bilingual experience is heterogeneous, and theories of experience-dependent adaptation should identify which dimensions of that experience are relevant to particular cognitive outcomes.

A theoretically motivated reanalysis might therefore improve on an earlier analysis if theory provides principled reasons for selecting different participants, constructing different indicators, or organizing those indicators into different latent dimensions.But theoretical motivation and theoretical constraint are not the same thing.
A framework can provide plausible reasons for making an analytic choice without uniquely-or even strongly-favoring that choice over alternatives.

The relevant question for theory testing is therefore not simply whether Navarro et al. could provide a theoretical rationale for each departure fromPaap et al. text.text: This distinction becomes important when considering the three major changes introduced in their reanalysis: restriction of the analytic sample, reconstruction of the bilingualexperience indicators, and reorganization of those indicators into multiple latent factors.Restricting the SampleNavarro et al. first restricted the original sample to participants they classified as bilingual, excluding participants at the relatively monolingual end of the bilingual-experience continuum.

This decision follows naturally from an interest in individual differences among bilinguals, but it is less obviously required by a theory proposing that accumulated bilingual experience alters domain-general cognitive functioning.

If the relevant mechanism is experience dependent, participants with little or no bilingual experience provide theoretically informative observations near the lower end of the putative dose-response function.

Removing them restricts the range of the presumed causal variable and changes the question from whether increasing bilingual experience predicts EF across the observed continuum to whether variation within a selected bilingual range predicts EF.

This distinction is especially relevant because Navarro et al. criticize the original sample for providing insufficient variability in bilingual experience: "the sample in this data set was largely imbalanced, and this was reflected in the lack of an effect from the proficiency factor (Factor 2) toward EF" (p. 12).
None of these observations requires the conclusion that Navarro et al.'s operationalizations are illegitimate.
Nor does our argument depend on proving that the Paap et al. measures were uniquely correct.
The more limited point is also the more important one: the changes do not establish that Navarro et al.'s analysis represents a uniquely theory-mandated improvement over the original analysis.
Several involve contestable measurement decisions, and the organization of those measures was partly informed by the observed data themselves.
Fortunately, the central empirical claim of the reanalysis does not require us to adjudicate all of these measurement questions.

We can grant Navarro et al. their restricted sample, reconstructed indicators, three-factor representation of bilingual experience, and specified structural model and ask a simpler question: When that model is reconstructed from the supplied code, does it produce the evidence for bilingualism-EF relationships reported in the article?
Reconstructing the Reported Analysis Navarro et al. (2026) addressed the substantial missing data in the EF measures using multiple imputation.
They report generating 20 imputed datasets with the mice package in R.

If greater experience exercising language control strengthens domain-general EF, the straightforward prediction would appear to be a positive relationship.
Yet the coefficient shown in Navarro et al.'s Figure 5, and reproduced in our reconstruction, is negative (β ≈ -.20).
